title: Beat √2−1: the zero-rate threshold for adversarial bit deletions
premise_risks: Could not read arXiv:2609.21395 (Sept 2026); title suggests it concerns code size for few deletions, but unverified
If p*=√2-1 the claim is false; posed as prove-or-disprove would also be fine
plain: A binary code of length n can correct pn adversarial deletions if no two codewords share a common subsequence of length (1−p)n. Let p* be the largest fraction for which there are codes of exponential size (positive rate). Simple pigeonhole shows p* ≤ 1/2. The best known constructions (Bukh-Guruswami-Håstad, 2015) give p* ≥ √2−1 ≈ 0.414, and the best upper bound is 1/2 − δ for a tiny unspecified δ. Decide whether p* > √2−1, i.e. whether there are positive-rate binary codes that correct more than a √2−1 fraction of deletions.
math: For $x,y\in\{0,1\}^n$ let $\mathrm{LCS}(x,y)$ be the length of a longest common subsequence. Let $p^*$ be the supremum of $p\in[0,1]$ for which there is $R>0$ and, for infinitely many $n$, a code $C\subseteq\{0,1\}^n$ with $|C|\ge 2^{Rn}$ and $\mathrm{LCS}(x,y)<(1-p)n$ for all distinct $x,y\in C$. It is known that $\sqrt2-1\le p^*<1/2$. Determine whether $p^*>\sqrt2-1$.
